newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Divisions still deep as Israel marks Rabin murder.
newsitem.headline: Divisions still deep as Israel marks Rabin murder.

text.p: Israelis marked the year anniversary of the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin on Thursday as divided politically as they were on the eve of the murder.

Thousands of people streamed to the Tel Aviv square where Rabin was murdered by a right-wing Jew after a peace rally a year ago. Schoolchildren marked the killing in a moment of silence on the anniversary according to the Jewish calendar.
But Israelis left and right were still sparring over the peace process Rabin embodied and the fate of Arab land the Jewish state occupies.
"The murder did not succeed in creating a common experience for all of the public. On the contrary, each side became more fortified in its position," said the newspaper Haaretz in an editorial.

Israel Television said on Wednesday dozens of legislaters had received death threats in recent weeks, including Shimon Peres, who succeeded Rabin after the November 4 assassination, and hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu defeated Peres in elections last May by less than 30,000 votes.

Rabin's landmark peace deals with PLO leader Yasser Arafat earned him the Nobel Peace Prize but made the Israeli leader and former war hero a traitor in the eyes of some right-wing Jews who view the West Bank as land promised the Jews by God.
The idea that a Jew would murder the prime minister of the Jewish state shocked Israelis but a year later left and right could not even agree on how to commemorate the assassination.

Israel's High Court ruled on Thursday against a petition to make the anniversary of the murder a national memorial day after right-wing legislators overruled the initiative in parliament that was put forward by a member of Rabin's Labour party.
Some Israelis felt the initiative was an attempt by the left to gain political mileage from the assassination.

At a memorial service planned for Sunday, members of the right-wing Betar and religious Bnei Akiva youth movements initially refused to sing the Song of Peace that Rabin sang at the rally where he was shot.
The song, which tells Israelis to forget past wars and usher in an era of peace, has become the left's mantra since the assassination.
"We aren't ready to accept the whole web of ideology of the left at face value because the prime minister, may he rest in peace, was murdered," said Betar leader Eldad Halahmi.
Israeli leaders and members of Rabin's family were due to attend a memorial ceremony at his grave in Jerusalem.

"I think that our obligation is to remember. To remember him and to remember his path, just to remember all the time...what he taught us all and what his death taught us," Rabin's granddaughter Noa Ben-Artzi said at a ceremony.
